heading: ## 05 — #7 THE MOAI, RAPA NUI (CHILE)
text: Number seven: the Moai of Rapa Nui, a remote Pacific island that is part of Chile. Nearly a thousand statues were carved here, most from one volcanic quarry, Rano Raraku. Most are a few metres tall, but some are huge. Paro, one of the largest ever erected, is estimated at around eighty tonnes. Rapa Nui tradition says the Moai walked. In twenty twelve, archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo tested that with a replica of about five tonnes. Eighteen people, three ropes, and the upright statue rocked forward, step by step. Statues abandoned along ancient roads fit that picture. It's a strongly supported explanation, but not proven for every statue, especially the heaviest. And in the quarry lies one giant, around twenty metres long, that was never finished. On Rapa Nui, the challenge was about a thousand statues. In Egypt, it was over two million blocks.
previous_text: Stonehenge's builders dragged their stones. On one Pacific island, people say the stones walked.
next_text: Number six: the Great Pyramid, built for the pharaoh Khufu around four thousand five hundred years ago. It originally stood about a hundred and forty-six point six metres tall, from an estimated two point three million blocks, its sides aligned to the cardinal directions with remarkable, though not perfect, accuracy.
